title: The Interior of the reservoir
premise: Rafael Ishikawa, a piano tuner who reads a house's past through its radiators and creaks, has spent decades keeping an inventory of everything unsaid—about her mother's disappearance, about the song her father wrote for someone who was never his wife. When she hears that unrecorded melody playing on a late-night radio program, credited to a stranger's name, the careful invisibility of her life collapses. Following the broadcast to a decaying lakeside house scheduled for demolition behind a new reservoir, she finds the composer's daughter, June, living among old photographs Rafael appears in as a child she doesn't remember being. As the sale deadline closes in, the two women excavate the truth: Rafael's mother wrote the song, gave it away to save her family, and vanished into the very valley soon to be flooded. To forgive the strangers in the photographs—and the mother who chose duty over her—Rafael must finally play the song aloud, ending not with the house's destruction but with its memory preserved in a recording made by two women who have become each other's found family.
about_author: Elodie Kavanagh is a former piano restorer who spent fifteen years tuning instruments in houses slated for demolition across the American West. She writes from a converted water tower in Oregon, where she keeps an inventory of everything unsaid.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Ear
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Working alone in a client's Victorian, she narrates how she hears history in pipes and floorboards, revealing her habit of cataloguing silences—her own most of all. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as competence; the reader learns she hasn't spoken to family in years.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. In her apartment she opens a battered notebook listing everything never said—to her father before he died, to her mother before she vanished. A radio left on drifts through static. Beat: quiet grief establishing what she stands to lose by staying invisible.

chapters.title: A Song That Was Never Recorded
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. At 2 a.m., the radio plays a melody she knows note-for-note—the lullaby her father hummed but swore no one had ever written down—credited to one 'H. Voss.' She calls the station; the DJ says the tape came from a listener in Alder Basin. Beat: shock cracking open her sealed life.

chapters.title: The Valley That Will Be Water
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, driving east. She researches Alder Basin: a town condemned, its valley to become a reservoir in ninety days. Maps show her childhood summer home inside the flood line. Beat: dread mixed with gravitational pull toward a place she fled at nine years old.

chapters.title: The House on the Draw
chapters.summary: Rafael arrives at the Voss house, half-packed for demolition, and is caught trespassing by June Voss, a brusque woman in her sixties sorting photographs. Beat: friction and mutual suspicion; June recognizes something in Rafael's face but says nothing.

chapters.title: Strangers in the Photographs
chapters.summary: June's POV. Alone, June studies a box of photos from 1970s summers: her father Henri with a dark-haired man at the piano—and between them, a small girl. She compares the girl's face to the trespasser's. Beat: recognition withheld, protective anger rising.

chapters.title: Terms of Entry
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. June offers a bargain: Rafael may search for the song's origin if she helps pack the house before the sale closes. Neither admits why they need the other. Beat: wary alliance built on mutual concealment.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Remember
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Tuning the house's ancient piano, she reads the building's thermal groans like testimony—a party, an argument, a door slammed on a winter night. She finds Henri Voss's composition notebooks, the lullaby written in her mother's handwriting beneath his signature. Beat: vertigo; the past is closer than she believed.

chapters.title: Henri's Side of It
chapters.summary: June's POV. June shares her father's letters: Henri loved Rafael's mother, Lena, and she loved him back, but both were married; when scandal threatened, Lena took the blame for a theft from the Ishikawa household and disappeared rather than destroy two families. Beat: June defends her father; Rafael hears her mother called a thief.

chapters.title: The Accusation
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Rafael accuses Henri of stealing Lena's song and her life; June accuses Lena of abandoning her daughter. The fight detonates the unsaid inventory. Rafael walks out into the first rain of the season. Beat: rupture—the alliance breaks along the fault line of their parents' choices.

chapters.title: Ninety Days Becomes Sixty
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Back home, she finds her mother's old letters to her father, unread for forty years, hidden in the piano bench of her own apartment—she'd been carrying the evidence all along. Beat: devastating irony; the answer was always within reach of her hands.

chapters.title: Lena's Letters
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, reading. The letters reveal Lena gave the song to Henri deliberately—a gift, a goodbye—and took the theft accusation to protect Rafael's father from ruin, then stayed away because returning meant watching Rafael be raised by the lie. Beat: grief reframed; duty and love were the same wound.

chapters.title: What June Kept
chapters.summary: June's POV. June unpacks her own sealed box: her mother's diaries admitting she knew about Henri and Lena, and chose to keep the marriage anyway—her own inventory of unsaid things. Beat: June's certainty cracks; she sees her mother's silence mirrored in her own bitterness.

chapters.title: The Reservoir Commission
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. At the county office she learns the sale can't be stopped, but historical designation could preserve the house's contents and record. The clerk needs proof of significance. Beat: hope with a deadline; the race now has rules.

chapters.title: An Uneasy Return
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Rafael returns; June lets her in without discussion. They work in silence, packing books, finding a 1974 reel-to-reel tape labeled only 'for L.' Beat: reconciliation without apology yet—tenderness expressed through shared labor.

chapters.title: For L.
chapters.summary: Both POVs. They play the tape: Henri and Lena recording the lullaby together, laughing, Lena singing a second verse neither ever performed again. Both women weep separately in the same room. Beat: the emotional summit of understanding; forgiveness becomes possible.

chapters.title: The Stranger I Was
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. In the photograph, nine-year-old Rafael stands between the two men, and she finally remembers that day—the last time all four adults were happy. She forgives the girl in the photo for forgetting, and begins drafting the letter to her mother she'll never send. Beat: self-forgiveness preceding the climax.

chapters.title: The Sale Closes
chapters.summary: June's POV. Escrow finalizes; movers arrive; the commission rejects the designation for lack of time. June signs away the house, then does something unplanned: she gives Rafael the piano and the tapes outright. Beat: sacrifice as inheritance; love against duty resolved in miniature.

chapters.title: One Last Tuning
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. On the empty house's final night, Rafael tunes the piano and plays the lullaby complete with the lost second verse while June records it on the old reel machine and a phone. The house holds the sound one last time. Beat: climax—the song finally recorded, the silence broken.

chapters.title: Water Rising
chapters.summary: Both POVs. From the ridge above the valley, they watch the reservoir gates close and the basin begin to fill. Grief and peace coexist; the house becomes lakebed, but the music survives. Beat: elegiac release; memory outlasting place.

chapters.title: A New Inventory
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Months later, Rafael mails the recording to the radio DJ, who plays it at 2 a.m.; listeners call in asking who wrote it. She answers, on air, with both names: Henri Voss and Lena Ishikawa. Beat: the unsaid finally said publicly; invisibility voluntarily ended.

chapters.title: The Interior of the Reservoir
chapters.summary: Both POVs, converging. June moves into the room above Rafael's workshop; they hang the photograph of four adults and a child on the wall. Rafael adds a final line to her notebook—not an unsaid thing, but a said one. Beat: found family secured; the story closes on warmth earned through loss.
